name: Nickle Green
lede: Nickle Green is a dark, greyish forest green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, one of four near-identical names the dictionary recorded for the same hue between 1912 and 1928.

sections.title: One hue, four names
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places this color at plate 31, chip E7, and dates its own first record to 1912 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system did not coin a separate name for it; it only cites Maerz and Paul's chip when classifying the color as a dark grayish green [1]. Our library notes three other dictionary names landing on the same chip at different dates: Juniper in 1919, Kabistan in 1925, and Frosty Green in 1928, so the trade named this one green at least four times in sixteen years [2].

In our color graph its closest named relatives are [[insect-screen]] and [[fir-green]], both within 3.3 units, with [[greyish-hunter-green]] and [[black-green]] close behind [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of Nickle Green covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 635 works, more common than 79 per cent of our named colors [4]. The 1900s carry it at 1.8 times the archive's overall rate, and Paul Cezanne returns to it in 8 of his 50 paintings here, about 4.2 times his museums' baseline [4]. It most often shares a canvas with Empire Green, at nearly 12 times the expected rate [4]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors [4].

questions.q: How many different dictionary names did Maerz and Paul record on this same color chip between 1912 and 1928?
True or false: the ISCC-NBS system gave Nickle Green its own independent classification, separate from Maerz and Paul's chip.

openers: Trade dictionaries named this same dark green at least four separate times in sixteen years.

issues: No source in our records documents why the name chose the nickel spelling "Nickle".
